removed_or_replaced_line: Artificial muscles are a key enabling technology for this class of robot. Among the available actuation technologies, McKibben-style braided pneumatic actuators (BPAs) combine low mass, high force-to-weight ratio, and intrinsic compliance with a force--length curve that qualitatively resembles that of skeletal muscle \citep{liang_comparative_2020, hunt_modeling_2017}. BPAs have been used in quadrupedal robots \citep{aschenbeck_design_2006, hunt_modeling_2017, scharzenberger_design_2019}, musculoskeletal humanoids \citep{asano_design_2017, hitzmann_anthropomorphic_2018}, and dexterous manipulation systems \citep{chen_realizing_2019}. However, BPAs also differ from biological muscle in important ways: their maximum tensile force occurs at resting length rather than at an optimal fiber length, their maximum contraction ratio is substantially lower than that of human muscle, and their force output is a highly nonlinear function of internal pressure, contraction, and loading state \citep{hunt_modeling_2017, sarosi_comparative_2017, liang_comparative_2020}. The author's experience with \qty{10}{\mm} actuators made this gap concrete: manufacturer specifications overstate the force and contraction available at the short resting lengths a leg design requires, and designs based on those specifications delivered less range of motion and joint torque than intended. Nor could the published empirical models repair the discrepancy, because each is fitted to measurements at a single resting length \citep{sarosi_comparative_2017, martens_modeling_2017, hunt_modeling_2017}; none accurately predicts how force changes when a designer chooses a different actuator length. Because muscle resting length is one of the primary degrees of freedom available to the robot designer, the absence of a force model valid at arbitrary resting length blocked rational actuator selection. Designing a biomimetic robot around BPAs therefore requires quantitative, predictive models of the actuator and of the joint torques it can produce.

There are additional gaps concerning the development of more detailed neural control models of locomotion and balance. One lies in the literature itself: the physiological properties of the group Ia, group Ib, and group II afferents that should inform the feedback design are scattered across a primary literature that the database of Chapter~\ref{ch:database} alone audits at 943 papers and reviews \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998, windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022}, with no structured resource from which a robot designer or an animal researcher could draw them. The other lies in methods: no simulation pipeline existed for closing the loop between a musculoskeletal robot model of this kind and a biologically grounded neural controller. The neuromechanical modeling literature provides the ingredients, including two-level spinal central pattern generator architectures \citep{rybak_modelling_2006, mccrea_organization_2008}, neuromechanical simulation frameworks \citep{markin_afferent_2010}, and synthetic nervous system design tools \citep{nourse_sns_2023}, but it does not provide their assembly for a BPA-driven bipedal robot with human-like muscle routing: the conversion of the robot's own model into a simulation engine, the wiring of the rhythm and reflex circuits with their afferent feedback, and the closed-loop coupling of controller and mechanics in one runnable environment.

The present work builds directly on a series of studies by me and my collaborators. In my master's project, the kinematics and dynamics of a biomimetic robot leg were matched against the Gait2392 OpenSim model, artificial muscle attachment and wrapping locations were determined for the robot legs, and MATLAB tooling was developed for evaluating muscle lengths, moment arms, and isometric joint torques over the full range of motion \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019, bolen_determination_2019}. That work showed that simply transplanting human muscle attachment locations onto a BPA-actuated robot does not reproduce human torque profiles; the placement optimization that closes this gap was completed during this dissertation and is summarized in Section~\ref{sec:foundation}. The rest of the platform advanced in parallel, and this dissertation builds on its hardware and demonstrations: the biomimetic four-bar knee linkage with a migrating instantaneous center of rotation, designed and validated by Steele \citep{steele_development_2017, steele_biomimetic_2018, steele_biomimetic_2018-1}, is the knee of the robot leg whose torque transmission Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} measures, and the canine-inspired quadruped platform Muscle Mutt, formerly called DoggyDeux, demonstrated antagonistic BPA pairs under synthetic nervous system control on a physical robot \citep{scharzenberger_design_2019}, extending an earlier AARL demonstration of central pattern generator control of a pneumatically actuated robot \citep{hunt_development_2017}. The humanoid leg of this dissertation carries that line forward.

This dissertation addresses the actuator-force and torque-correction gaps experimentally, resolves the afferent-data gap by consolidating the afferent literature into the Sensory Afferent Database \citep{bolen_sensory_2023, bolen_using_2024}, and closes the simulation-pipeline gap with the tools and framework of the final research chapter. The objectives are:

Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} develops and validates the actuator force models. It presents the isometric force characterization of Festo BPAs with \qtylist{10;20}{\mm} uninflated diameters over a wide range of resting lengths, contractions, and pressures; derives improved maximum-force and normalized force--strain--pressure models; and compares them against the manufacturer's tool and published models. Later sections examine the effects of resting length, the implications of the validated models for real-time control and simulation, and the biomimetic analogy between braided pneumatic actuators and skeletal muscle. The chapter's text and figures are adapted from my publication of this work \citep{bolen_2026}.

The moment arm is the quantity that turns muscle force into joint torque, and two methods of obtaining it anchor the literature. The geometric method computes the arm directly from attachment-point data: the arm about a joint axis is the perpendicular distance from that axis to the muscle's line of action, evaluated at the configuration of interest. \citet{brand_model_1982} assembled the canonical lower-extremity attachment anatomy from cadaver measurements so that such computations could be made at all, and reported that anatomical variation and marking errors rarely shift calculated moment arms by more than twenty percent, usually by less than ten, while attachment data taken from a single unscaled specimen can bias the resulting force predictions substantially. The tendon-excursion method instead defines the arm as the sensitivity of musculotendon length to joint angle, $r = \partial l/\partial\theta$, obtained by perturbing a joint and differencing path lengths. \citet{menegaldo_moment_2004} fitted polynomial regressions of musculotendon lengths and three-dimensional moment arms across the joint space of a lower-limb model so that either quantity could be evaluated cheaply inside large simulations. Both methods deliver configuration-dependent quantities rather than constants, and the dependence compounds for multi-articular muscles, whose arm about one joint varies with the configuration of every joint they cross \citep{zajac_determining_1989}; the full-muscle rat hindlimb model of \citet{young_analyzing_2019} makes that adjacent-joint dependence a primary result of its attachment-point technique. OpenSim evaluates moment arms as muscle-length sensitivities of this kind, so the moment arms used in the robot model's design and torque predictions here are properties of the Gait2392-derived geometry rather than quantities measured on the robot \citep{delp_opensim_2007, seth_opensim_2018}; the torques measured on the test stands of Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} are the experimental ground truth against which those geometry-based predictions are checked.

The human knee is the joint where the choice of these definitions matters most. Its instantaneous center of rotation migrates posteriorly with flexion, a behavior captured by four-bar linkage descriptions of the joint \citep{romero_four-bar_2020, steele_biomimetic_2018}. Locating that moving center is a kinematic problem in its own right, and \citet{romero_four-bar_2020} solve it with natural coordinates so that the answer stays cheap to evaluate when an optimization must recompute it many times. The difficulty is visible at the repository level: the SimTK repository that distributes OpenSim also hosts multiple projects dedicated specifically to the human knee, and they differ in how they formalize joint torques, centers of rotation, and reaction forces for the same anatomy. A hinge knee, a four-bar knee, and a contact-defined tibiofemoral joint give different moment arms for identical muscle paths, so the modeling choice must be determined carefully. Gait2392 resolves the knee with planar kinematics \citep{yamaguchi_planar_1989}: the flexion angle prescribes the joint's translation as well as its rotation, rather than fixing a hinge axis or solving a linkage. The ISB joint coordinate system recommendations were written to resolve exactly this definitional freedom, keeping reports of joint motion comparable across laboratories \citep{wu_isb_2002}. Throughout this dissertation, Gait2392 serves as the reference against which the robot's muscle routing, moment arms, and torque capabilities are designed and judged.

The mechanics of that study are worth stating precisely, because Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} builds on them. Moment arms were computed geometrically from attachment points in the body frame, as the cross product of a joint-axis unit vector with the vector from the joint center to the muscle's line of action, as described in Section~\ref{sec:bg_biomechanics}, and isometric torque was calculated as muscle force multiplied by moment arm, evaluated across each joint's range of motion. The comparison the study made was robot against human: each PAM's origin, via points, and insertion were placed by hand in OpenSim beside the Gait2392 path it imitates, adjusted so that the contraction each actuator must produce over the range of motion stays within the Festo BPA's usable contraction range and so that actuators do not interfere with one another, and the resulting robot model, gait2392\_robotbody, is the robot model whose torque transmission the later chapters of this dissertation refine \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019}. The biceps femoris long head shows what the robot-versus-human comparison exposed: its path differs visibly between the two models as the knee flexes, and the robot model's knee- and hip-axis torque surfaces reach only a fraction of the human model's peaks over the hip--knee range. Profiles of this kind, read across the full muscle set, defined the matching problem that the placement optimization later formalized \citep{morrow_optimization_2020}. Figure~\ref{fig:masters_routing_and_arms} shows the routing models and the moment-arm construction, and Figure~\ref{fig:masters_torque_comparison} shows the biceps femoris comparison.

Computational neuroscience expresses hypotheses about neural circuitry as executable models. A computational model is a system of coupled equations in which elements of the schematic correspond to identified neural populations or pathways, so a published wiring diagram can be read as a specification of the model itself, not merely as an illustration of it. The locomotor circuits of Section~\ref{sec:bg_neural}, from Brown's half-center \citep{brown_intrinsic_1911} through the two-level architectures and their muscle-coupled extensions, are the executable models this tradition has produced; this section treats the tradition, and Section~\ref{sec:bg_sns} the tools that carry it to robots.

One way of interpreting computational neuroscience diagrams is from a controls tradition in which the block diagram is the controller itself. Each block is an identifiable neural population with conductance-based dynamics, and each connection is a synaptic conductance with a physiologically interpretable weight. The controller developed in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} comes from this tradition: its two-layer organization follows the rat hindlimb model of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019}, and its verification tests are drawn from the deletion and stimulation phenomena that the models of \citet{rybak_modelling_2006} and the air-stepping experiments of \citet{selionov_tonic_2009} explain.

The boundary between background and contribution runs through this section as well. The prior AnimatLab walker with which my program first applied these architectures to a biped \citep{bolen_design_2020} is presented as prior work of this dissertation in Section~\ref{sec:prior_walker}, the Sensory Afferent Database that organizes the afferent data such networks require \citep{bolen_sensory_2023} is the subject of Chapter~\ref{ch:database}, and the simulation pipeline that couples the controller to the robot model is built in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}. None of it is repeated as background here.

For a robot to serve as a replacement subject, however, it must first earn standing as a scientific model. Webb's influential analyses of bio-robotic methodology \citep{webb_robots_2001, webb_robots_2002} argue that a robot is a good model of biological behavior when the mechanism it implements is tested at the same level of organization as the target phenomenon, matching dynamics, control structure, and sensory ecology rather than surface appearance. The validation chain of this dissertation is constructed to that standard: the actuator force model is validated against bench data (Section~\ref{sec:results_force}), the joint torque model against isometric measurements and human torque envelopes (Section~\ref{sec:results_torque}), and the neuromechanical controller is verified against published tonic stimulation and deletion phenomena \citep{selionov_tonic_2009, rybak_modelling_2006}, the verification step that precedes locomotion tuning in this program. Only then can a robot experiment be read as evidence about the hypothesized biological circuit rather than about the robot.

The route redesign built on these values addresses the single-muscle shortfall at high flexion angles documented in Section~\ref{sec:results_torque}: each configuration now carries two \qty{20}{\mm} BPAs per route. The extensor route has since been redesigned once more by allowing the tibial-side route points to trace a cam profile, and this cam redesign is the current extensor design. The cam solution converts the razor-thin margin of the direct route into genuine design headroom. On the final geometry, which folds the optimizer winner together with a verified adjustment of the distal route point and tendon length, the minimum torque margin is $+30.83\,\%$ with respect to the required envelope, the human target plus the 5\,\% overshoot, and $+39.77\,\%$ with respect to the plain human target; the optimizer winner before that adjustment carried $+31.30$\,\% and $+42.34$\,\% at the same checks. The pressure required to meet the envelope spans \SIrange[range-phrase=--]{269}{507}{\kPa} across the range of motion, comfortably above the \qty{150}{\kPa} regulated floor of the VTUG valve manifold that supplies the hardware. The geometry confirms that the headroom is not bought with routing risk: the tibial wrap follows a bend radius of \qty{96.9}{\mm}, the guiding route point clears the femoral-condyle envelope by \qty{43.1}{\mm} at \ang{10} of knee extension, and the moment arm spans \SIrange[range-phrase=--]{59.4}{102.8}{\mm} (mean \qty{72.4}{\mm}) over the range of motion.

The same redesign pipeline was then extended from the knee to all 27 muscle-actuators of the robot-body model, and this whole-body extension is reported as work in progress rather than a completed result. The first pass reached 19 of the 27 actuators before the run stopped, and its chosen solutions showed that the penalty-based formulation itself was the binding limitation: all but one of the chosen routes violated the feasibility constraints, the sole exception being the biceps femoris long-head pair, whose worst-angle margin of $+0.03\,\%$ is indistinguishable from zero. The formulation was then restructured so that the task envelope, the joint-angle window each route must serve, acts as a hard feasible set rather than a penalty. In the restructured pass, twelve of the 27 actuators terminated on a concatenation error in the route builder (the three lumbar-wall actuators, tibialis posterior, the seven distal-foot actuators, and adductor magnus), leaving fifteen finalized routes. Eight of the fifteen were chosen from constraint-feasible configurations: semimembranosus, biceps femoris long head, tensor fasciae latae, soleus, lateral gastrocnemius, tibialis anterior, iliacus, and psoas. Of those eight, six also met the torque requirement at every angle, with worst-angle margins spanning $+0.25\,\%$ (biceps femoris long head) to $+250.7\,\%$ (tensor fasciae latae); the semimembranosus and soleus routes satisfy the geometry but remain short of their torque targets. The crash set and the two torque-short feasible routes define the remaining engineering: the route builder needs a fix for the concatenation failure, and the short routes need either larger actuators or relaxed corridors.

I built it within the AARL's NeuroNex Communication, Coordination, and Control in Nervous Systems (C3NS) effort and presented it at Neuroscience 2023 \citep{bolen_sensory_2023}, and later presented the AI-assisted triage study that expanded it at Neuroscience 2024 \citep{bolen_using_2024}. Its content is organized as five linked tables (Papers, Feedback, Models, Review Papers, and Recorders), with the DOI as the unique identifier wherever a record carries one. The Papers table is the core: each paper carries structured curation notes, one to three sentences of distilled mechanism written from the paper's own text, never from memory, with free-text fields constrained by controlled vocabularies for animal preparations and afferent classes. Each sensory feedback pathway is a record in its own right in the Feedback table, named by a fixed grammar of afferent, action, side, joint, and phase (for example, ``Ib stance to swing''), so that pathway records compose into circuits the way a controller will use them, and each is linked to the papers that established it. The Models table links each computational model of afferent control to its source paper and to the pathway records it implements, and the Review Papers and Recorders tables carry the review literature and the instrumentation papers behind the electrophysiology.

The database answers queries that no bibliography can. A designer can filter the corpus by afferent class, animal preparation, or pathway; follow a pathway record to the papers that established it in each species; walk the citation neighborhood of a candidate anchor paper; or count the corpus along any two dimensions at once. The database's primary form is the packaged explorer: a single-file, offline application embedding the full audited corpus, its citation graph, and its named topic clusters, with searchable and pivotable tables, focus-mode citation neighborhoods drawn in the laboratory's own convention of papers as neurons, and a generated knowledge base with cluster, pathway, afferent, and animal pages, running in a browser on any machine with no network connection (an off-the-shelf bibliometric viewer was tried first and retired within weeks: no drill-through from a cluster to its papers, and a handful of mega-cited classics dominating every view). The working Airtable base remains the editable home of curation, but it cannot travel past the laboratory's account, and every build of the explorer embeds the corpus whole, including the papers the prune archived from the working base. This section records what a reader needs to know to understand how the corpus was assembled and judged: the sources it came from, the rules a record had to satisfy, the role of the AI tools, and who decided. The reviews this dissertation draws on mark the starting point rather than the method: \citet{van_de_crommert_review_1998} organize the sensory control of the central pattern generator, \citet{windhorst_muscle_2007} assigns functional roles to muscle proprioceptive feedback, and \citet{windhorst_spinal_2022} weighs accumulated spinal-circuit model assumptions against the experimental record. Each synthesizes a slice of the literature; none can be filtered by afferent class, animal preparation, or pathway, none carries its demonstrating papers as attached and followable evidence, and each is fixed at its publication date.

The corpus was assembled from three sources that did not agree: my personal Zotero collection (538 items), the AARL group library's Biology subtree (911 items across 27 collections), and the Airtable base (99 papers). Matching record by record on DOI and normalized title showed that the personal collection was essentially a subset of the group library and that the Airtable base was a small curated subset rather than a mirror, and the gap was imported in verified batches, each written record re-read and checked after writing. The corpus then grew through citation mining, newly saved references, and a bulk pass that imported 372 papers auto-classified from the laboratory's staged PDF collection, bringing the audited corpus to 943 papers, the full set against which every later decision in this chapter was made.

The curation was machine-assisted under a division of labor in which the machine drafts and the human rules; the comparative evaluation of the AI tools that motivated this division is reported in Section~\ref{sec:sadb_triage} \citep{bolen_using_2024}. The machine contributed scale: batch drafting from grounded text, automated vocabulary, abstract-paste, and duplicate gates that rejected bad records before anything was written, and per-record verification against the grounding text after the write. I held every decision that required judgment or carried risk: the curation vocabulary and its amendments, the 164 flagged judgment calls, and every single deletion in the prune. Papers for which no text could be found stayed bare by rule rather than guessed, with grounding recovered where the laboratory's own library or a university-authenticated session could provide it.

Pruning then removed 436 records, 382 papers plus 54 orphaned review, model, and pathway records, in three stages: off-topic satellites, duplicates, and orphans first; a rule-built cut list of 290 papers next, ranked by a weighted rubric over citation count, age, rating, network isolation, and record thinness, with 351 protected records (foundational authors, feedback-linked papers, highly cited work, and pre-1940 classics) excluded from consideration; and a final sweep of records whose links the earlier cuts had emptied. The prune was deliberate on two grounds: the working base stood at 1,393 records before the prune, the 943 papers of the audited corpus plus 450 linked review, model, pathway, and recorder records, swollen past the laboratory's free-plan record cap; and a curated resource that answers a design question in ten records beats a haystack of a thousand. No record was destroyed; every deletion was snapshotted, and the packaged explorer carries the 382 cut papers under an archived flag, so the audited corpus remains reconstructible in full.

At the close of the curation effort the working base held 957 records: 561 papers, 39 feedback-pathway records, 244 model records, 109 review records, and 4 recorder entries. Coverage of the retained papers is concentrated where the laboratory's design and experimental work needs it. Of the 561 retained papers, 523 carry curation notes, 426 carry animal-preparation tags, 240 carry notes assessing each paper's animal-study potential, 118 are linked to named feedback pathways, 86 carry an afferent classification, and 258 carry notes translating the paper's findings toward robot or simulation use; 550 carry DOIs, and 38 remain bare pending a findable text.

The citation graph was built over the full audited corpus of 943 papers, which includes the 382 records the prune later removed. Within that corpus, 730 papers are connected by 11,130 directed in-corpus citation pairs, and a Louvain community partition of the graph resolves 18 named topic clusters, from the classics of afferent locomotor control and spinal interneuron circuit modeling through human balance and posture to bioinspired flow sensing and deep-learning methods. The partition earned its keep in the prune: the satellite clusters it exposed, the flow-and-flight sensing, fish swimming, and neural-network method clusters, match the topic groups the first prune stage removed. Within that audited corpus, 833 papers carry curation notes and 318 carry attached PDFs. The corpus, its citation graph, its cluster assignments, and the flat corpus export are distributed together in the packaged explorer.

Expanding a curated corpus is dominated by triage: deciding, paper by paper, what a record is about and whether it belongs. I evaluated AI tools for this task in a comparative study presented at Neuroscience 2024 \citep{bolen_using_2024}. The evaluation found the expected trade: the tools accelerated the population of the database, but their output still required substantial human oversight for accuracy. The curation workflow of Section~\ref{sec:sadb_methods} is the operational answer to that finding. Its gates earned their place on caught failures, including a record that shipped another paper's abstract under its title until the grounding pass flagged it; the human rulings it reserves are the oversight the evaluation showed was necessary, made concrete.

The preceding chapters validate the robot's mechanics: a force model for the braided pneumatic actuators (Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles}) and a corrected model of the joint torque those actuators deliver through the biomimetic knee (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}). This chapter builds the other half of the neuromechanical system, the controller, together with the simulation tools required to develop it. The controller is a synthetic nervous system (SNS): a network of conductance-based neuron and synapse models whose organization follows the mammalian spinal cord \citep{rybak_modelling_2006, mccrea_organization_2008, deng_neuromechanical_2019}. Its parameters are not trained in the machine-learning sense but set from physiological data and tuned against explicit verification tests, which keeps every neuron an identifiable cell class and lets the simulated system support lesion, stimulation, and sensory-deletion experiments that cannot be performed on living subjects (Section~\ref{sec:bg_ethics}). The neural vocabulary, the two-level central pattern generator, and the afferent channels are defined in Sections~\ref{sec:bg_neural}--\ref{sec:bg_sns} and used here without redefinition; the neuron and synapse equations themselves are recorded in Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations}.

As preliminary work of this dissertation, built before the simulation toolchain of this chapter existed, Morrow and I combined two published designs into a neuromechanical model of a bipedal walker in AnimatLab, a graphical environment for building biomechanical systems actuated by synthetic neural systems \citep{cofer_animatlab_2010}: the biomechanics came from the suspended bipedal walker of \citet{li_bipedal_2017}, and the controller from the two-layer CPG organization of \citet{deng_neuromechanical_2019}. That combination is the direct ancestor of the work reported here: its biomechanics and its controller architecture carry through every model in this chapter, and the limitations of its hand-tuned parameters are the reason the present toolchain emphasizes systematic verification.

The synthetic nervous network was built from non-spiking, leaky-integrator neurons. A rhythm-generator layer set the timing of the system; a pattern-formation layer reshaped the timing signals into phase-appropriate activation of antagonist muscle groups; and a sensorimotor layer containing Renshaw-cell-like recurrent inhibition drove the motor neurons. The sensorimotor layer received Ia (length and velocity) and Ib (tension) afferent feedback from the muscles, but the feedback gains were never systematically tuned, and no ground-contact signals were modeled. Every applied current, synaptic weight, and muscle-tension parameter was set by hand: each was adjusted by trial and error, one at a time, until the three layers oscillated in phase and the motor neurons produced stepping-like activation of the muscle pairs. That hand-tuning consumed the bulk of the project's effort, left no record of the sensitivity of the behavior to individual parameters, and did not generalize when new feedback pathways were added. It produced alternating, stepping-like motion with the walker suspended in the air, presented at the 2021 NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting \citep{bolenTorqueValuesArtificialKnee2021June15-17}, but it never produced walking: no hand-set combination of parameters bore the robot's weight, and the feedback pathways were never exercised under load. Those outcomes directly motivated the verification-first approach of the remainder of this chapter.

First, no environment coupled neural control to the models this program works on. The two-level controller existed only in AnimatLab projects; it had never been coupled to a full human-scale musculoskeletal model such as the Gait2392 model, nor to the robot-body model with its BPA muscle routing, and AnimatLab carried neither. MuJoCo, SNS-Toolbox, and the conversion tools existed as separate pieces with no assembled path between them \citep{todorov_mujoco_2012, nourse_sns_2023}.

Third, there was no graphical circuit construction on maintained simulation tools. The circuits of this lineage are block diagrams, and building them by hand in code is slow and hard to inspect; a block-programming environment such as Simulink is the natural medium, and Simscape Multibody additionally accepts CAD-derived bodies. The predecessor SNS block libraries of this laboratory's own lineage \citep{hunt_development_2017, young_analyzing_2019} did not carry the elements the robot requires, and no current library did.

None of the infrastructure components is invented here: OpenSim supplies the musculoskeletal modeling side, the robot's source model, and the moment-arm and torque standards the conversions are audited against \citep{delp_opensim_2007, seth_opensim_2018}; MuJoCo supplies the physics engine \citep{todorov_mujoco_2012}; MyoConverter performs the base OpenSim-to-MuJoCo conversion \citep{caggiano_myosuite_2022, wang_myosim_2022}; SNS-Toolbox builds and integrates the spinal networks \citep{nourse_sns_2023}; AnimatLab hosts the controller lineage's archived reference models; Simulink and Simscape Multibody supply the controls-engineering environment; and SCONE provides the reference point for mature predictive neuromuscular simulation \citep{geijtenbeek_scone_2019}, whose published balance and gait demonstrations were reproduced headless as a practice baseline and whose balance tutorial anchors the standing stage of the training curriculum (Section~\ref{sec:sns_curriculum}). The sensory channels that close the loop, and the acceptance phenomena against which the controllers are validated, trace to the curated records of the Sensory Afferent Database of Chapter~\ref{ch:database} (Section~\ref{sec:sadb_use}).

The SNS block library stands in a direct lineage, and the comparison matters. The SNS formalism descends from the block-based Simulink libraries of this laboratory's own research line, in which \citet{hunt_development_2017} trained the hindlimb-walking neural controller and with which \citet{young_analyzing_2019} built and analyzed a full-muscle rat hindlimb model; those libraries drive Hill-type biological muscles on animal-scale models. The Simulink tool is a block library, built so that synthetic nervous systems can also be assembled and inspected in a standard controls-engineering environment. Seven core blocks, a graded neuron, a graded chemical synapse, a spiking leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, Ia and Ib afferent encoders, muscle activation dynamics, and a generic BPA force block, implement the same equations as the SNS-Toolbox networks; diameter-specific BPA force elements (\qtylist{10;20;40}{\mm}) implementing the fitted force surfaces of Chapter~\ref{ch:methods} and a Hill-type muscle element complete the library, which runs in base Simulink without additional toolboxes (Figure~\ref{fig:simulink_sns_implementation}).

Making the controllers and bodies portable is the third tool family. The Deng two-layer CPG was rebuilt as separate editable Simulink files with the published parameter tables carried over \citep{deng_neuromechanical_2019, nourse_sns_2023}; one cell-level choice proved load-bearing for portability, a burst-termination property of the rhythm-generator cells whose membrane mechanism is recorded in Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations}. In the other direction, a script turns the tuned production network into an editable Simulink model built from the library blocks, one per neuron and one per synapse, regenerating whenever the tuning changes. Two body-import routes bring real geometry into Simscape Multibody: the SolidWorks knee via URDF and Multibody-Link XML, and the OpenSim \texttt{gait2392\_simbody} model via MuJoCo and URDF, with the massless muscle path-point slides preserved as links so that actuators attach at the same physical points as in the source; a URDF carries no muscles, so actuation re-enters as SNS library blocks driving the imported joints. A MuJoCo--Simulink bridge block set closes the loop from the Simulink side, muscle activation commands in and joint and actuator sensors out.

The verification harness, a fixed script suite that re-runs and checks the models, is a tool in its own right, and its fundamental demonstration is replication in two forms: the same rhythm core rebuilt in two engines must reproduce the same rhythm, and the lineage's archived models must reproduce their published behavior in their original engine. The harness is defined around the contact-driven rhythm core of the Walker-2-Layer (W2L) bipedal architecture, four rhythm-generator populations, one extensor and one flexor population per leg plus graded pattern-formation and sensory cells, driven by heel-contact mechanosensory feedback \citep{deng_neuromechanical_2019}. The same core was implemented twice from a common connectivity specification, once as a NumPy reference through the SNS-Toolbox backend and once as native Simulink blocks, and both were driven with an identical protocol scored on burst period, left--right antiphase, burst counts, and full-trace correlation. The archived AnimatLab reference models were additionally re-run headless from their standalone simulators, so that engine-level and network-level agreement could be separated.

The final tool tests an assumption rather than adding a simulation capability. The controllers documented above compute with graded (non-spiking) neurons; to test that the conclusions drawn from them are not artifacts of graded coding, spiking mirrors of all three simulation families were built under one design rule: the motor-neuron layer stays non-spiking, because the musculoskeletal model consumes a continuous activation command, while the afferent encoders, rhythm-generator populations, and interneurons become leaky integrate-and-fire neurons operating at real membrane-potential ranges \citep{szczecinski_perspective_2023, nourse_sns_2023}. The MuJoCo mirror reproduces the production spinal network population for population, is selected at build time by a single environment-variable switch, and leaves the default build path untouched, proven by re-running its defaults gate and baseline evaluation to bit-exact agreement; because SNS-Toolbox 1.5.2 ships no spiking bursting-neuron class, its rhythm-generator populations are adapting integrate-and-fire cells. The mirrors' synaptic weights are set by a calibration script, not by hand, calibrated by mean conductance onto the motor neurons and by firing-rate transfer between spiking cells, with the full calibration tabulated in Appendix~\ref{app:neuron_equations}. In the Simulink family, three blocks were added, a \texttt{SpikingNeuron}, an event-wired \texttt{SpikingSynapse}, and a \texttt{HybridSpikingSynapse} carrying the same conductance dynamics onto a non-spiking postsynaptic cell, and spiking twins of the demonstrations replace only the sensory interneuron layer. In the AnimatLab family, a conversion script rewrites spiking copies of the runnable standalone exports, leaving every original untouched. Each mirror is verified against its non-spiking twin by a fixed gate set, topology (identical connection multiset), rhythm within \qty{20}{\percent} of the analog period, a basin gate under \qty{1}{\percent} multiplicative jitter on every scalar parameter, and regression to the committed artifacts, and carries mapped parameters only, with no new tuning, so its results establish what transfers structurally and what requires re-tuning.

Above the physiologically set values, the free gains of each network are tuned by systematic search rather than by hand: a sequential model-based optimizer (a tree-structured Parzen estimator) proposes gain sets, each proposal is scored by a full simulation, and each stage's winner seeds the next. No hand-tuned parameter enters a production configuration; the failure mode of the prior walker was precisely hand tuning that left no record of sensitivity. Robustness is enforced during tuning rather than inspected afterward: finalist configurations must retain their rhythm under \qty{1}{\percent} multiplicative jitter on every scalar parameter, survive stepping of the tonic drive about the tuned value, and, for standing configurations, absorb push perturbations without falling. The requirement exists because the tuned networks sit near bifurcations of their dynamics, as the spiking results of Section~\ref{sec:spiking_results} make explicit. The reference data for tuning and evaluation are inverse-kinematics cycles from many human subjects of different sizes and speeds rather than a single subject: a 43-cycle locomotion reference library, detailed in Section~\ref{sec:gait_library_results}. Circuit structure is treated as data under the same methodology: every network's connection multiset is compared programmatically against its intended topology, and the publication schematics are generated from the compiled network with each drawn edge asserted against the compiled connection list.

What spiking does not change is the behavior of the controlled model, provided the design rule and the calibration hold: because the motor-neuron layer stays non-spiking and the spikes onto it are calibrated by mean conductance, the continuous activation interface that the actuator and torque models of this dissertation attach to is unchanged by construction. The Simulink twins make the point quantitatively, with the knee-reflex settle band moving by \ang{0.9} and the beverage-holding reflex modulation by \ang{0.02}. The actuator-level and joint-level conclusions of Chapters~\ref{ch:methods}--\ref{ch:results} therefore do not depend on the neural coding chosen above the motor-neuron layer.

What spiking changes is timing and robustness. The mirror's self-sustained rhythm runs \qty{55.6}{\percent} slower at the same constant drive, and its air-stepping cadence runs roughly ten times faster, deviations in opposite directions, which a single scaling error could not produce; the constant-drive period traces to two identifiable knobs, the threshold-increment magnitude and the adaptation time constant, so a period-matched spiking controller is a short tuning effort away rather than a structural failure. Robustness moves in the mirror's favor: the spiking rhythm-generator populations passed the perturbation basin gate in full where the analog network's rhythm sits close to a bifurcation, and for the hardware-transfer program of Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework}, where the network will be re-implemented in finite-precision arithmetic, a wide basin is the safer substrate. What spiking does not tolerate is a naive parameter copy at the synapse level: the AnimatLab conversions show that converting graded amplitudes to per-spike increments of the same magnitude breaks the reciprocal rhythm-generator loop, while converting only the thresholds changes nothing; synaptic strength in a spiking network is a rate-code quantity that must be derived from the presynaptic firing rate and the conductance decay, exactly as the calibration script derives it. The one place where the untuned mirror outperforms its tuned twin, a bilateral ground gait where the winner's left leg is frozen, is a single run with no statistics, claimed only as a lead for the closed-loop CPG comparison program of Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework}.

The tuned configurations of this chapter were not tuned all at once. The training proceeds through five stages (Figure~\ref{fig:sns_curriculum}), each adding one capability and seeded with the previous stage's winner so that only the newly activated pathway gains are searched: deafferented air stepping first, afferented air stepping second, standing balance third, ground walking fourth, and ground walking with the contact-driven pathway variant fifth. Standing before walking is the design rule: gait tuning begins only after a configuration holds posture, and the failures the curriculum surfaces early are the cheap ones. The scoring is stage-appropriate and gated: rhythm and swing depth for the air stages, with the objective rhythm-gated so a frozen configuration cannot win by holding a pose; posture maintenance under push for the balance stage; and the cycle-shape kinematic score for the walking stages. The walking score is rhythm-gated in the same way for a subtler reason: a run with no detectable gait cycles returns a fixed sentinel ($-25$) rather than a score, because that sentinel sits numerically above every genuine gait score, and reading it as a score would let a frozen model out-score a walker. Scores are never read alone: finalists must pass the perturbation and basin requirements of Section~\ref{sec:sns_tuning_methods}, because a score achieved on a narrow basin is a property of the solver rather than of the circuit.

The actuator model travels with the controller: inside the MuJoCo loop, actuator force comes from the quasi-static BPA model of Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} with the correction-factor force balance of Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}, and in Simulink the library's diameter-specific force blocks implement the same fitted surfaces, so every closed-loop demonstration in this chapter draws its forces from one validated source. What the integration does not yet carry is actuator dynamics: the pressure--force dynamics under pulse-modulated valve control \citep{elzein_pressure_2025} enter the program as future work (Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework}).

The end-to-end demonstration of the MuJoCo chain, conversion pipeline plus force interface plus network builder, is the BPA-actuated robot. The walker geometry of Section~\ref{sec:prior_walker} was exported to MuJoCo and driven by antagonistic BPA actuator pairs under the split contact-driven network, with actuator forces computed by the BPA model. In the air-stepping preparation, with the harness carrying 70\% of the \qty{411}{\N} body weight, the walker produced clean knee-flexion excursions at a \qty{1.542}{\second} period with a knee flexion range of \ang{63.5}, peak BPA forces of \qty{880}{\N} (left) and \qty{1372}{\N} (right) at a peak pressure of \qty{372}{\kPa} (60\% of the \qty{620}{\kPa} ceiling), and 7 and 5 heel-contact episodes on the left and right: the complete chain from the characterized BPA force model to a multi-joint walker stepping under synthetic neural control.

The same evaluation series reported its failures with equal weight. On the ground, the W2L gate model under its untuned default gains stands (full-support stance) but does not walk: heel duty is zero and forward displacement is $+\qty{0.001}{\meter}$ over the run. With the left and right drives separated and the feedback gains re-tuned, the same robot alternates in antiphase (inter-leg phase 0.487) and progresses \qty{1.72}{\meter} over a \qty{30}{\second} window (\qty{0.066}{\metre\per\second}) under the harness protocol, with the neural drive weaned to \qty{60}{\percent} of its bootstrap value and the result robust under perturbation (12 of 12 basin re-runs); below \qty{60}{\percent} drive the gait dies, the harness itself is not weaned, and foot duty remains below the strict walking gate, so the result is supported progression rather than validated walking. The MuJoCo re-implementation of the Li model produced no stance episodes in any of seven drop-protocol variants. Together with the latch result of Section~\ref{sec:crossengine_results}, these negatives localize the open problem precisely: the contact-driven rhythm architecture itself transfers across engines intact, but translating it to unsupported ground locomotion requires the balance and weight-bearing layers defined in Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework}, and those layers are not present in these models.

The walking status deserves a precise statement, because the chapter's records support exactly this and no more. Each tuned configuration was brought through the curriculum's air and balance stages, and on the ground all walking evaluations run under the support harness, where the configurations produce gross walking-like progression with right-leg-only or asymmetric gait patterns. A subsequent drive-weaning study re-tuned the feedback gains while forcing the hand-drive down a ladder of scales: its finalist improves the default build's evaluation score from $-161.57$ to $-145.07$ with a bilateral gait of ten contact cycles per leg (contact duty 0.71 and 0.65), survives a closed-loop basin check in eight of eight perturbed evaluations, and, with its feedback held fixed, keeps bilateral stepping at every drive scale down to zero hand-drive, at which the drive pathway is absent from the network entirely, whereas the un-retuned configuration collapses below \qty{85}{\percent} of full drive. The gait remains in-place alternation under the support rig, without forward progression. Unsupported, harness-free walking has not been demonstrated anywhere in this program's records, and whether any configuration walks without the harness is an open question; the balance and weight-bearing layers that would answer it are the first item of the simulation program defined in Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework}.

On the converted robot-body model, the four production walking configurations span the controller lineages, and scored with the same cycle-shape kinematic score against the 43-reference library, the family-level fact is that the robot-walker-lineage configuration, not the human-derived ones, agrees most closely with the library, while the six-synergy configuration, the most strongly human-derived in its pattern formation, agrees least closely; closing that gap is a tuning-program question rather than a tool question. On the physical-model side, the SolidWorks knee assembly is imported into Simscape Multibody with its degree-of-freedom defect documented and its fix defined, and the imported \texttt{gait2392\_simbody} mechanism awaits its muscle blocks; neither physical model yet carries a tuned controller.

Attachment and routing optimization is the second enabler, and it is tiered. The placement optimization of Morrow, Bolen, and Hunt found artificial muscle attachment locations that reproduce human torque profiles and ranges of motion about the trunk and leg joints \citep{morrow_optimization_2020}, converting the earlier finding that transplanted human attachment locations do not transfer directly to a BPA-actuated robot \citep{bolen_bipedal_2019, bolen_determination_2019} into a usable design tool; the route redesigns of Section~\ref{sec:ongoing} rerun that machinery under the corrected torque model. At the route-selection tier, with two \qty{20}{\mm} BPAs per route and routes chosen with the actuators' bending in mind, the redesigned flexor and extensor each meet or exceed the magnitude of their human-scaled torque targets across the full knee range of motion, and the cam-profile extensor converts the direct route's thin margin into genuine design headroom (Section~\ref{sec:route_redesign_results}). Stated as a design program, the generalization is one or more BPAs replacing one or more human muscles across one or more joints, serving the two degrees of freedom that matter most at each joint, with routes grown outward from positions close to the bone and held to the spatial constraints of the candidate actuators and of the BPAs already mounted; the first whole-body pass over the robot's actuator set, with its successes and its failures, is reported in Section~\ref{sec:ongoing}. Where the attachments are fixed and only the route and the tendon length can change, the cam-shape solver applies: the tibial-side route points trace a designed cam profile, trading biomimicry for torque-profile optimization and reduced component forces.

The Sensory Afferent Database (SADb) is the third enabler (Chapter~\ref{ch:database}). It organizes the sensory-afferent literature into a structured afferent resource \citep{bolen_sensory_2023}: of the 561 papers retained after the audit and the prune, 523 carry structured curation notes, 86 carry an afferent classification, and 258 carry notes translating each paper toward robot or simulation use, and the full audited corpus of 943 papers, including the 382 pruned records preserved under an archived flag, remains reconstructible in the packaged tool. The toolset matters as much as the corpus. Its detailed table drills from any filter down to a paper's full notes; its pivot view counts the corpus along any two dimensions at once; its bubble map draws every paper as a neuron, soma sized by citations, with citation links rendered as excitatory and inhibitory synapses in the laboratory's convention and a focus mode that walks the citation neighborhood; and the monthly skimmer--curator workflow sweeps the recent literature for candidate records and routes every one of them to a human ruling. The evaluation of AI-assisted literature triage established the division of labor that makes expansion affordable \citep{bolen_using_2024}: the machine drafts, and the human rules.

The fourth enabler is the set of novel neuromechanical simulation tools (Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}): the audited OpenSim-to-MuJoCo conversion of the robot's musculoskeletal model, the force interface that computes actuator forces inside the loop from the validated BPA model, the two-level spinal networks built in SNS-Toolbox, the Simulink SNS library for assembly in a controls-engineering environment, the cross-engine verification harness, and the spiking-neuron mirrors that test the coding assumption. On these tools the controller program has matured from assembly into use. Production walking configurations have been tuned and evaluated in full-body ground simulations, the first pathway-deletion and drive-stimulus experiments have been run, the gait-validation sweep has measured how far the tuned networks remain from the diversity of human reference locomotion, and the contact-driven rhythm core has been shown to transfer between independent implementations with exact period agreement and trace correlations above 0.9999. In hardware, the companion balance-platform studies demonstrated that a BPA-actuated limb holds itself upright under pseudo-vestibular inertial feedback \citep{bolen_balance_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_srs_2024}. What remains unfinished is equally specific, and it organizes the future work below: the balance and weight-bearing layers that unsupported bilateral walking requires, wider transfer across reference cycles, the supraspinal sensorium, and embedded real-time execution.

The database's growth now has two engines: the monthly skimmer--curator workflow that sweeps the recent literature, and machine-assisted drafting under human ruling. The next step the corpus itself suggests is prompt-driven passes over the existing records, designed to discover the notes and rules latent in the corpus, candidate pathway records, missing cross-links, controlled-vocabulary amendments, and gaps in the afferent classification, and to draft entries for the flagged stubs and for the vocabulary gaps that the extensions of Section~\ref{sec:fw_senses} will need first, vestibular and visual preparations among them. Two constraints from the curation rules carry over unchanged. The passes must be economical and their accuracy measured against human rulings rather than assumed, and a human still rules on every write; the triage evaluation found acceleration with substantial oversight required \citep{bolen_using_2024}, and nothing in the pipeline removes the evaluator. What the passes buy is coverage at the corpus's edges, at a cost a laboratory can afford.

The simulation laboratory of Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} is assembled, audited, and in active use. The converted robot model carries all of its muscle-tendon actuators with audited geometry, and the BPA force interface computes actuator forces from the validated model inside the loop; both are documented as complete in the chapter's methods (Section~\ref{sec:preliminary_sim_methods}). The 410-neuron SNS-Toolbox instantiation of the spinal network, with per-leg rhythm-generator half-centers, phase-shifted pattern-formation groups, motoneuron pools for every actuator, and Ia, Ib, and II afferent populations, couples to the converted model at a \qty{2}{\milli\second} neural step, and production walking configurations have been tuned against a walking reference and evaluated on the ground (Section~\ref{sec:gait_library_results}). A drive-weaning study has since produced a feedback-sustained bilateral configuration whose stepping persists with the hand-drive withdrawn entirely, still in place under the support rig, and the robot-side model progresses under its harness at weaned drive (Section~\ref{sec:sns_controller_comparison}). What those same evaluations localize as missing defines the work remaining here: the balance and weight-bearing layers that unsupported, bilateral walking requires; transfer from a single tuning reference to the diversity of the locomotion reference library; and the systematic verification series that follows.

The verification series comes first because it is cheap and decisive. The circuits' signs, gains, and phase structure are checked against the experimental literature with the stimulus protocols the physiology itself uses: a tonic stimulus applied at the motoneuron, pattern-formation, and rhythm-generator layers, with the resulting outputs compared against the tonic central and sensory stimulation that facilitates involuntary air-stepping in humans \citep{selionov_tonic_2009} and the deletion and stimulation phenomena reproduced by the two-level CPG models and their neuromechanical implementations \citep{rybak_modelling_2006, markin_afferent_2010, shevtsova_modeling_2016}. The first of these tests is complete at the rhythm-generator level, where tonic drive evokes an approximately \qty{0.9}{\second} antiphase cycle in the isolated network (Section~\ref{sec:preliminary_sim_methods}); the motoneuron-level and pattern-formation-level series remain to be run, together with the motoneuron skipping-deletion phenomenon of the reference models.

Once stepping is stable, three supraspinal contributions will be added, and a fourth is in line behind them (Figure~\ref{fig:sensorium_hierarchy}). First, vestibular feedback will be simulated with IMU-like sensing of body orientation and angular velocity, extending the balance-platform work, in which an inverted pendulum with pseudo-vestibular IMU feedback maintained balance on an oscillating platform \citep{bolen_balance_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_srs_2024} and analytic neural networks reproduced human balance dynamics \citep{hilts_dynamic_2019}. Second, ocular feedback will be modeled to investigate how visual stabilization cues can help reset IMU drift, a well-known practical problem for inertial sensing on robots, by treating visual measurements of the horizon and surroundings as a low-frequency correction to the vestibular estimate. Third, a cerebellar layer will be explored as an adaptive gateway between higher-level locomotion commands and the CPG: a structure that can gate between gaits or movement patterns (e.g., walking, running, and turning) and tune the phase relationships among them, in line with the cerebellum's established role in adaptation and coordination. Multilevel spinal-plus-cerebellar synthetic nervous systems have already been demonstrated for insect-like legs \citep{grummer_multilevel_2024}, and hierarchical cortico-cerebellar-spinal models have been proposed for adaptive step-length control in bipedal locomotion \citep{chen_corticocerebellar_2025}. The fourth addition, basal-ganglia circuits realizing the inhibitory and excititory gating that selects among actions and locomotor modes, would give the controller a substrate for choosing between behaviors rather than only executing one. The database already holds the entry points for this program: the human balance and posture cluster and the multisensory recalibration cluster are curated and connected to the locomotor core through the citation graph (Chapter~\ref{ch:database}), and the proprioceptive--vestibular interaction literature will guide how the signals are weighted \citep{akay_relative_2021}.

Beyond the specific models, the dissertation's methodological contribution is the actuator-to-joint design chain itself: characterize the actuator, correct for the compliance and geometry of the transmission, validate against human biomechanics, and only then close the loop with a controller. The neural layer that completes the chain is assembled rather than absent: the converted MuJoCo model, the SNS-Toolbox coupling, and the two-layer spinal network with its verified antiphase rhythm generator are already in place. The portability of these neural primitives was verified directly: the contact-driven rhythm core reproduces with exact period agreement and trace correlations above 0.9999 between independent NumPy and Simulink implementations, the archived AnimatLab reference models reproduce their published rhythms headless, and a BPA-actuated walker in MuJoCo air-steps under synthetic neural control, while the honest negatives of the same evaluation series localize the remaining gap in the balance layer, not in the rhythm, the actuators, or the engines.
